title: Two years after her son's shooting death by Calgary Police, First Nations mother wants change
article: A still grieving Chiniki First Nation mother is calling on the Calgary Police Service (CPS) to review its threat assessment training.
Lena Wildman believes her son would still be alive if there were changes in how officers learn to assess threats and de-escalate risky situations.
"There's so much force used on our people-there's no danger-they need to change their threat assessments," Wildman says.

Wildman's son Levon Boyce Jackson Fox, 39, a member of the Goodstoney First Nation in the foothills west of Calgary, was shot and killed by CPS on May 29, 2023. Fox had two older brothers and two younger siblings, including a sister he was especially close to.
Wildman is waiting patiently for the outcome of the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team's (ASIRT) investigation into the shooting, but wants to see change now.
APTN News reached out to ASIRT for an update on its investigation, but have so far not heard back.

ASIRT'S initial news release of the incident said police had received multiple reports of an alleged impaired driver operating a stolen five-ton cube van. It was "driving erratically in a manner that was dangerous to the public throughout northeast Calgary," ASIRT said.

Police first learned of the incident when a "security guard called police regarding three suspicious and impaired individuals on private property. It is believed the individuals fled the scene in the five-ton van, colliding with a building and a barricade in the area as they sped away," according to the ASIRT release.
Officers located the van heading westward at slow speed on Calgary's Memorial Drive.
"To prevent the van from entering the busy downtown core or neighbouring residential areas, multiple police units were called in to block intersections and bridges along Memorial Drive," ASIRT said.

After the vehicle made a sharp U-turn, "officers made attempts to conduct a traffic stop, which were unsuccessful. Despite the vehicle driving at low speeds at that time, the driver continued to swerve across all lanes of traffic and refused to stop,"

A number of police vehicles were accompanying the vehicle, but the van was able to break containment and continued moving towards officers, according to ASIRT, and "a 13 year member of the CPS discharged their service firearm."
In one video seen by APTN News, the van is driving slowly down the street with a half dozen police cars following behind. Later in the video, the van disappears from view and shots ring out.
According to Wildman, the driver who was not Indigenous, and her son were killed, while her older son who was on the passenger side was not injured and taken into custody.
The shooting happened near one end of the Reconciliation Bridge.

"I've finally looked at the video-there's lots of different recordings of it online," Wildman says. "You can tell that the vehicle had stopped and they were never even given the opportunity to get out of the vehicle, they were just shot."
Wildman says the men were not armed and did not show any weapons.
APTN asked the CPS about threat assessments and it provided a statement.

"De-escalation and Use of Force training begins in recruit class and officers must requalify through in-service training on an annual basis. De-escalation, specifically, is threaded throughout our in-service training, which happens throughout the year and covers many different topics," the statement from the CPS says.

"The Service also utilizes a De-escalation and Use of Force Framework that illustrates the elements involved in how an officer assesses a situation and acts to ensure officer and public safety," the statement notes. "This includes bringing more visibility to how each call for service is approached and highlighting the value placed on de-escalation. Rather than prescribing specific techniques or responses, the Framework focuses on training officers in adaptive decision-making."
The death of Wildman's son was made all the more tragic because she says, he was trying to turn his life around.
"My son that passed away, he was on the path to breaking away from the addiction to these hard drugs," Wildman says. "He had been to detox and he was on medication."
She says he was living in Edmonton with her at the time, for the resources and supports he could get for detox and addiction.

But, Wildman says her son visited Calgary because he worried about his older brother, who has "been in a life of addiction for so many years, and is still struggling today." She said Fox had indicated he wanted to come home to Edmonton and said he'd let her know when to pick him up.

Wildman is planning a walk to commemorate her son's passing on May 29. It will start at the Calgary Tower at 11 a.m. and end near Reconciliation Bridge and the site of the shooting. They'll have a meal and ceremony.

"The first year, according to our teachings, I've been quiet and I've been still. Taking care of myself in prayer and ceremony. If it wasn't for prayer and ceremony, I don't know how I would've made it through a year," Wildman says.
"There are days when it's unbearable."
